title: Koko Eating Bananas
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential speed testing versus binary search on the eating speed, using total hours needed as a monotonic feasibility check.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Koko has piles of bananas, piles[i] being the number of bananas in the i-th pile. She eats at a constant speed of k bananas per hour: from a pile, she eats k bananas that hour, or if the pile has fewer than k, she finishes it and stops for that hour. Given h total hours available, return the MINIMUM integer speed k such that she can eat all bananas within h hours.

blocks.text: As the eating speed k increases, the total hours needed to finish all piles can only decrease or stay the same, never increase. This monotonic relationship between speed and total time is exactly the structure that makes "binary search on the answer" applicable, searching directly over candidate speeds.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Slowest Acceptable Reading Pace
blocks.text: Picture needing to finish several books within a deadline, where reading faster (more pages per hour) always finishes each book in fewer or equal hours. You want the SLOWEST acceptable pace that still meets the deadline, since reading unnecessarily fast is undesirable. Binary searching over candidate paces, checking if each meets the deadline, finds this efficiently.

blocks.caption: A faster eating speed always needs fewer or equal total hours, a monotonic relationship enabling binary search

blocks.text: Result: 4. At speed 4: ceil(3/4)+ceil(6/4)+ceil(7/4)+ceil(11/4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours, exactly fitting within h=8.

Before testing speeds sequentially from 1 upward, notice that the total hours needed is a monotonically NON-INCREASING function of speed, which is exactly the signal for binary searching directly on the candidate speed, checking feasibility (hours needed <= h) at each step.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: At a given speed k, the hours needed for a single pile of size p is ceil(p / k), since any remainder still requires one more hour to finish that pile.

Observation 2: Summing ceil(p/k) across all piles gives the TOTAL hours needed at speed k, a function that is easy to compute directly in O(number of piles).

Observation 3: As k increases, ceil(p/k) for each pile can only decrease or stay the same, so the total hours needed is monotonically non-increasing in k.

Observation 4: This monotonicity means binary search can directly find the smallest k for which the total hours needed is <= h, narrowing the search range based on whether the current candidate speed is fast enough.

This leads to binary searching over candidate speeds k in [1, max(piles)], computing the total hours needed at each candidate (an O(number of piles) computation), and narrowing toward the smallest feasible speed.
Try speeds 1, 2, 3, ... in increasing order, computing the total hours needed at each, stopping at the first speed where the total is within h hours.

items: Starting from speed 1, compute the total hours needed (sum of ceil(pile/speed) over all piles).
If this total is at most h, return this speed.
Otherwise, increment the speed and repeat.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every speed in order directly finds the smallest feasible one, guaranteed correct.
This could require up to max(piles) iterations, potentially very slow given piles can be as large as 10^9.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(max(piles) times number of piles), checking every speed sequentially.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: since the total hours needed is monotonic in speed, binary search finds the minimum feasible speed in O(number of piles times log(max(piles))) instead of a full linear scan over speeds.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sequential speed testing is slow: with piles up to 10^9 in size, testing every speed from 1 upward could take up to a billion iterations.

The binary search insight: since increasing speed can only decrease (or keep the same) the total hours needed, this is a classic monotonic feasibility function, exactly the structure binary search on the answer exploits.

Defining the feasibility check: for a candidate speed k, compute sum of ceil(pile/k) over all piles; if this total is <= h, speed k is feasible (search for a possibly smaller feasible speed); otherwise it is infeasible (search for a larger speed).

The core idea: binary search directly on the candidate speed, using the monotonic total-hours-needed function as the feasibility check.
Binary search speed k in [1, max(piles)]. At each step, compute the total hours needed at speed k; if <= h, move hi to k (searching for a possibly smaller feasible speed); otherwise move lo to k+1.

blocks.caption: Binary search on speed, using the monotonic total-hours-needed function as the feasibility check

blocks.text: Since the total hours needed is a monotonically non-increasing function of speed, the binary search invariant holds: if a candidate speed is feasible (hours needed <= h), a smaller speed might still be feasible, so the search continues in the lower half (inclusive); if infeasible, every smaller speed is also infeasible, so the search must move to a larger speed. This converges exactly on the minimum feasible speed.

items: Using floor division instead of ceiling when computing hours needed per pile, undercounting the hours for piles that do not divide evenly by the speed.
Searching speed starting from 0 instead of 1, since a speed of 0 would never finish any pile.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum rate/speed to finish within a time limit", think: binary search on the rate, using a monotonic feasibility check (time needed at that rate).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sequential speed testing costs O(max(piles) times number of piles) time; binary search on speed costs O(number of piles times log(max(piles))) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer (speed), using a monotonic feasibility check (total hours needed).
Core Idea: binary search speed k; compute total hours needed (sum of ceil(pile/k)); narrow toward the smallest k with hours needed <= h.
Time: O(max(piles) times number of piles) for sequential testing, O(number of piles times log(max(piles))) for binary search.
Most Important Observation: speed and time-needed have a monotonic (inverse) relationship, enabling binary search directly on the speed.
Interview Difficulty: a very well-known and frequently reused "binary search on the answer" template problem.
One line memory trick: binary search the speed; sum ceil(pile/speed) as the feasibility check.
